title: Classification and regression applied to business problems

videos.script: Lesson 13 defined churn by looking backwards: a customer silent for forty-two days has probably gone. A model looks forwards. It reads what is known about each customer today and estimates who will be gone in three months. {{forwards}} That is classification: every customer gets a probability, and somebody chooses where to draw the line between "contact them" and "leave them alone". {{classification}} Panela's model will be right nine times in ten. That sounds excellent, and it is the least useful thing to say about it, because a model that predicts nobody leaves is right eight times in ten. {{accuracy}} What matters is how many of the leavers it finds, how many of its alarms are real, and what each mistake costs. {{costs}} The same machinery predicts a number instead of a category. How much will this customer spend next quarter? That is regression, and it is judged like the forecasts of lesson 5, against the simplest guess. {{regression}} This lesson builds both, on a test that only uses the past to predict the future. {{end}}
